faqs.question: Can you redesign my existing website?
faqs.answer: Yes. I begin with the content, URLs, features, and integrations that need to stay. The redesign scope then covers what changes, how existing pages are redirected, and how the new site will be reviewed before replacing the current one.

faqs.question: Will the website work on mobile and with a keyboard?
faqs.answer: Responsive layouts and keyboard checks are part of the implementation. We agree on the important browsers and devices, then check navigation, forms, focus states, and content at those sizes. A formal accessibility audit can be scoped if you need one.

faqs.question: Can I update the website myself?
faqs.answer: Yes, when content management is included. We identify which areas need editing, who will publish, and whether changes require approval. The handover covers those tasks so routine updates do not depend on remembering how the code works.

faqs.question: Can you work from an existing design?
faqs.answer: Yes. I can build from supplied designs after checking responsive states, interactions, content, and reusable patterns. Missing error, empty, or mobile states are clarified before implementation so the build has a complete set of requirements.

faqs.question: Can the website connect to my CRM, booking system, or payment provider?
faqs.answer: I review the provider's supported interfaces, account access, and test environment first. The integration scope includes field mapping, successful and failed requests, and who resolves exceptions after launch.

faqs.question: What determines the price and delivery schedule?
faqs.answer: The main factors are page templates, content readiness, custom interactions, integrations, and review cycles. I use those details to propose milestones and a fee. Hosting, licenses, and other third-party costs are identified separately.

faqs.question: Is SEO included in the build?
faqs.answer: The build can include descriptive metadata, semantic headings, crawlable links, and an agreed redirect plan. Keyword research, ongoing content work, and a wider technical SEO engagement are separate scope decisions.

faqs.question: What happens after launch?
faqs.answer: You receive the agreed deployment and editing handover. We also define who handles hosting, updates, backups, and incoming issues. Ongoing maintenance or additional features can be arranged separately with explicit availability and response expectations.

faqs.question: Should I build custom software or use an existing product?
faqs.answer: We compare the workflow fit, integration effort, licensing, and ongoing ownership costs. An existing product may cover most of the need. Custom development makes sense when a specific requirement justifies the cost of building and maintaining it.

faqs.question: Can we start with an MVP?
faqs.answer: Yes. We define the assumption the MVP needs to test and a complete journey for its first users. Features that do not support that learning can wait, while essential permissions, data handling, and operational needs stay in scope.

faqs.question: Can you take over an existing application?
faqs.answer: I start with a review of the stack, code structure, dependencies, deployment, and current issues. That review establishes whether I can contribute effectively and what must be addressed before committing to new features.

faqs.question: Who owns the source code and accounts?
faqs.answer: Code ownership, usage rights, and account access are recorded in the agreement before work begins. The handover identifies third-party licenses, services, and dependencies so you can understand what you own and what needs an ongoing subscription.

faqs.question: How do you handle changing requirements?
faqs.answer: We keep a visible backlog and discuss changes against the current milestone. If a new requirement affects cost, timing, or another feature, we agree on the trade-off before treating it as part of the delivery commitment.

faqs.question: How is quality checked?
faqs.answer: Checks follow the risk and scope of the application: relevant automated tests, manual workflow reviews, permission checks, and deployment validation. You review working software against agreed acceptance criteria throughout the build.

faqs.question: How are cost and timing estimated?
faqs.answer: The estimate depends on workflows, integrations, data complexity, and unresolved decisions. For uncertain projects, a discovery phase can establish a realistic first milestone. Larger builds are split into releases that can be estimated and reviewed individually.

faqs.question: Can you maintain the software after delivery?
faqs.answer: Maintenance and further development can be agreed separately. The arrangement should define availability, issue reporting, release responsibilities, and the difference between correcting an issue and adding a new capability.

faqs.question: Do we need to rewrite the whole application?
faqs.answer: That decision follows the assessment. Targeted upgrades, refactoring, or replacing a module may resolve the main constraint. A full rewrite needs a clear benefit, a realistic transition plan, and a way to preserve business behavior throughout the move.

faqs.question: Can feature development continue during modernization?
faqs.answer: It can, if responsibilities and dependencies are planned together. We agree on which parts are changing, how releases are coordinated, and how compatibility is checked so product work does not invalidate the modernization effort.

faqs.question: What if there are no tests or useful documentation?
faqs.answer: I begin with walkthroughs, representative data, and a bounded set of checks around critical behavior. The initial work may focus on understanding the system and establishing a safety net before making structural changes.

faqs.question: Can you work with older PHP or Laravel applications?
faqs.answer: I can assess them after reviewing the versions, dependencies, codebase, and hosting. The review establishes viable upgrade paths and any constraints that need additional specialist support before committing to the implementation.

faqs.question: How do you protect existing data?
faqs.answer: We plan backups, migration rehearsals, mapping rules, and reconciliation checks for the affected data. Changes that alter stored information need a recovery strategy that accounts for new writes, not only a code rollback.

faqs.question: Will users need to change how they work?
faqs.answer: Only where the agreed scope changes their workflow. I involve users in reviewing those changes and document the new process. Training and the switch from old to new behavior are considered before rollout.

faqs.question: How do we choose the first modernization step?
faqs.answer: Prioritize a bounded change that addresses business risk or repeatedly blocks useful work. Dependencies, release constraints, and the ability to verify the result all influence the order.

faqs.question: How are cost and timing estimated for an unfamiliar system?
faqs.answer: An assessment helps uncover the parts that are difficult to estimate from a brief alone. I then propose a first milestone with explicit assumptions and review points. Further stages are updated as the system becomes better understood.

faqs.question: Can the application move without downtime?
faqs.answer: The achievable cutover window depends on the architecture, data store, and synchronization options. We establish a realistic target during planning and test the steps that affect it. Zero downtime is not assumed as part of every migration.

faqs.question: Will moving to the cloud lower our costs?
faqs.answer: It may or may not. We compare the current setup with destination costs such as compute, storage, transfer, backups, and monitoring. Expected usage and ongoing operating effort matter as much as the advertised price of a server.

faqs.question: Do we need to rewrite the application?
faqs.answer: Some workloads can move with configuration and deployment changes; others need application changes. The assessment separates migration requirements from optional modernization so the cutover does not take on unnecessary complexity.

faqs.question: Which provider will you use?
faqs.answer: We review your existing accounts, team skills, regional requirements, integrations, and workload needs. Implementation scope is confirmed for the chosen environment, including any work that needs a dedicated infrastructure specialist.

faqs.question: How do you check the transferred data?
faqs.answer: Checks are agreed for each data type. They may include counts, checksums, relationship checks, sample records, and application workflows. We also plan how to reconcile data written during the transition.

faqs.question: What happens if the cutover fails?
faqs.answer: The runbook includes stop conditions, recovery owners, and a fallback path. If new writes have reached the destination, recovery must account for those changes. A code rollback alone is not treated as a complete data recovery plan.

faqs.question: Who runs the environment after migration?
faqs.answer: We name the operational owner before cutover and hand over the agreed deployment, monitoring, backup, and escalation procedures. Ongoing managed operations or on-call coverage require a separate arrangement.

faqs.question: What determines the migration schedule?
faqs.answer: Dependencies, data volume, transfer limits, destination readiness, and rehearsal findings all affect timing. A fixed business deadline should be discussed early so the sequence and cutover window can be planned around it.

faqs.question: Can you work with the systems and data we already have?
faqs.answer: Yes, after reviewing access, formats, source ownership, and quality. The first milestone can use existing databases, exports, or APIs where they are suitable. Replacing every source system is not a prerequisite.

faqs.question: Do we need a data warehouse?
faqs.answer: That depends on the number of sources, data volume, transformations, access patterns, and refresh needs. We choose an architecture for the actual reporting requirements rather than adding a warehouse by default.

faqs.question: Can the reports update automatically?

faqs.question: Does my workflow need AI?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. If inputs and decisions are predictable, rules and standard integrations may be enough. I consider AI where interpretation is useful and assess whether its accuracy, review effort, and operating costs suit the task.

faqs.question: Can you connect the tools we already use?
faqs.answer: I first review supported APIs, webhooks, authentication, permissions, rate limits, and test access. The workflow can only promise actions those systems allow. Where a supported connection is missing, that constraint is made explicit before implementation.

faqs.question: How do you deal with incorrect AI output?
faqs.answer: The design uses structured outputs, business-rule checks, representative evaluations, and review queues where needed. Formatting checks alone cannot establish factual accuracy, so source verification and the impact of an error influence how much review is required.

faqs.question: Can the automation make changes without asking a person?
faqs.answer: Only for actions explicitly approved in the scope. Consequential changes can require human approval, and the workflow's access is limited to the operations it needs. Pause controls and a clear exception path are part of the design.

faqs.question: What happens to the data sent to a model provider?
faqs.answer: We review what information is necessary, which provider is involved, and your requirements for processing and retention before implementation. Redaction or a different deployment approach may be needed. Production data is not the default starting material for a pilot.

faqs.question: How will we know if the pilot is worth continuing?
faqs.answer: We agree on a manual baseline and compare completion, errors, review effort, and running costs. The pilot should show whether the complete workflow is useful, including the human work required to keep it dependable.

faqs.question: What ongoing costs should we plan for?
faqs.answer: Possible costs include model usage, hosting, storage, integration subscriptions, and operational review. I document the usage assumptions and monitoring needs so the cost of running the workflow is visible alongside the build fee.

faqs.question: Can the workflow be changed or paused after launch?
faqs.answer: Yes, within the controls included in the implementation. The handover explains how to pause processing, review failed jobs, and change agreed settings. Larger changes to prompts, models, or permissions should be checked against the evaluation cases before release.

Forms accept an enquiry, but nobody can confirm it reached the CRM.
Button clicks and successful submissions are counted as the same result.
after: Keep the offer, audience, and next step consistent across the journey.
Validate delivery, assignment, confirmation, and failure handling.
Define and test distinct events for the actions the business needs to measure.

process: Discuss the campaign audience, offer, primary action, and the people responsible for media, creative, approvals, and technical delivery.
Review the current landing journey, form behavior, event setup, consent requirements, and destination workflow. Identify gaps that affect launch readiness.
Agree on the page content, conversion definition, field mappings, event plan, and acceptance checks before implementation.
Build and test the scoped experience across relevant devices. Verify successful and failed submissions, lead delivery, and the agreed tracking behavior.
Complete the handover and review available visitor and lead-quality feedback. Further experiments follow an agreed hypothesis and measurement plan.

faqs.question: Do you manage advertising accounts and budgets?
faqs.answer: My primary scope here is landing pages, integrations, and technical measurement. Media buying, budget decisions, and ongoing account management need a separate, explicit agreement. I can work alongside the person or agency already responsible for those activities.

faqs.question: Can you build a landing page for an existing campaign?
faqs.answer: Yes. We agree on the audience, approved offer, content, primary action, and launch requirements. The page can connect to your current forms, CRM, or other supported destination systems.

faqs.question: Can leads go directly into our CRM?
faqs.answer: Where the CRM provides a suitable integration, the flow can include field mapping, validation, source information, and assignment. Failed deliveries need a visible recovery path so a successful form response does not hide a lost enquiry.

faqs.question: What counts as a conversion?
faqs.answer: We define that together before adding tracking. It may be a confirmed enquiry, completed registration, or another meaningful action. A button click is recorded separately when it does not prove that the intended outcome happened.

faqs.question: Will reporting match perfectly across every platform?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Different event definitions, attribution rules, consent choices, and incomplete data can produce differences. The implementation documents what each signal represents and which limitations need to be considered when comparing reports.

faqs.question: How do you handle consent and tracking requirements?
faqs.answer: You provide the approved tracking and data-handling requirements. I implement the agreed behavior and verify event firing under the relevant consent states. Decisions about what data may be collected are established before tags or integrations are enabled.

faqs.question: Can you guarantee more leads or a return on ad spend?
faqs.answer: No fixed return is promised. The offer, audience, creative, campaign settings, follow-up, and market conditions also influence results. The engagement is scoped around the technical work, its validation, and any agreed experiment.

faqs.question: Are media spend, creative, and software subscriptions included?
faqs.answer: They are separate unless explicitly listed in the agreement. The proposal identifies the development scope and dependencies, including campaign assets, tracking tools, CRM access, hosting, and any required paid services.
